issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessed domestic violence, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile unless there is some additional perpetration or morally injurious behavior by the patient during the trauma. In this profile there are no memory or threat items indicating the patient did something blameworthy during the event, so this item is clinically hard to explain.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: 'Being criticised or corrected' can occur in many PTSD presentations, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and appraisal items center on fear/safety, grief, and self-instability rather than interpersonal criticism or humiliation. Given the specified trauma and the other items selected, this trigger appears insufficiently linked to the formulation and surrounding symptoms.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For childhood witnessed domestic violence, strong self-blame can occur, but the specific wording 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with a witness-child trauma unless there is some indication she directly intervened or was held responsible. The rest of the profile does not suggest that role, so this item is clinically questionable for this trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: Avoiding open or exposed spaces implies a danger formulation centered on attack in public/exposed environments. The rest of the profile's triggers and memories are strongly interpersonal/domestic (shouting, touch, body odour, grief, visual memories of domestic violence), and the threat items emphasize checking safety/startle rather than fear of exposed outdoor space. This avoidance strategy does not fit the dominant trauma-linked threat pattern and is the least coherent item cross-node.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 39-year-old Latina detective who grew up in a household where violence was a nightly possibility. Her father was a large, physically imposing man whose rages arrived without warning - one moment the kitchen smelled of sweat and beer, and the next her mother was against the wall, her father's voice filling every room in the apartment. Valentina was seven the first time she watched this happen in full, crouched behind the sofa, and she would go on watching for the next decade: the particular smell of her father's body after he came in from the heat, the way a raised hand or sudden movement across the room could mean everything was about to change, the shouting that seemed to compress the air itself. These were the textures of her childhood, and they lodged somewhere deeper than conscious memory.

She left home at eighteen, built a career in law enforcement through what she described as sheer stubbornness, and for years managed to keep the past at a functional distance. But in the months following a domestic violence callout two years ago - a scene that replicated her childhood apartment with an accuracy that felt almost deliberate - the distance collapsed. The memories returned not as narrative but as images: her mother's face at a particular angle, a hand raised in silhouette, fragments that arrived without sequence or context and left her flooded with a grief she could not locate or name. When she tried to deliberately recall what had happened in her childhood, the memories became slippery and inaccessible, as though her mind refused to grant her the coherence she sought. This quality of the memory - vivid in pieces, unreachable as a whole - left her feeling that something was profoundly wrong with her.

She had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that the event had happened because of the kind of person she was - that there was something in her nature that invited harm, that made her unworthy of safety. This belief did not stay abstract. It fed directly into her sense that she could not trust herself to act correctly, and that her current reactions - the hypervigilance, the intensity of her distress - were evidence that she was losing her grip on reality. These appraisals sharpened the grief that came with every memory fragment, making recall feel not just painful but confirmatory: each image seemed to prove the worst things she thought about herself. And paradoxically, the appraisals kept her sensitised to the very triggers she feared - she moved through the world already certain that danger was her inheritance, which meant that sweat, sudden movement, a raised voice felt not incidental but inevitable.

At work, this had become impossible to manage quietly. As a detective, Valentina regularly encounters scenes of domestic disturbance, and the smell of a suspect's body odour or the sound of shouting in a corridor would send her system into full alert - heart rate spiking, every muscle braced, the threat response indistinguishable from what she had felt as a child. These moments of activation led her to hurt herself physically, pressing her nails hard into her palm or later, at home, more deliberately, because the sharp focus of physical pain was the only thing that interrupted the cascade. She had also begun refusing all physical contact - colleagues who reached for her shoulder in the break room were met with a step back and a tight smile - and she had organised her life around emotional flatness, avoiding anything that might produce feeling in either direction. She chose seats in every room - squad briefings, restaurants with her partner - based on sightlines and exits, and she woke most nights to check her apartment, certain something had shifted. Yet these strategies, rather than steadying her, had begun to erode the ground beneath her. The self-harm and the emotional numbing kept her from processing what she carried, leaving the memory fragments as raw as ever, and her partner had begun to name the distance between them. Her avoidance confirmed, in her own mind, that she was not coping - which deepened her conviction that she was going crazy, which in turn made the vigilance feel more necessary, the triggers more unbearable.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment in the precinct parking lot: a male colleague jogged past her unexpectedly, and she spun and had her hand on her weapon before she knew what she was doing. She stood there afterward, shaking, and thought: I cannot keep doing this job this way. What she most fears is that the therapy will confirm what she already suspects about herself. What she most hopes, though she has not yet said it aloud, is that it will not.
